### What issue are you seeing?

I’m seeing several cross-platform inconsistencies with a shared ChatGPT Project that appear to be related.

Environment:
- ChatGPT mobile app: project works normally
- ChatGPT web: project works normally
- ChatGPT desktop app: NEW ChatGPT desktop app, not ChatGPT Classic
- Same ChatGPT account across surfaces

Expected behavior:
The shared project should appear normally in the Projects section of the desktop app, and opening one of its chats should display it in the standard full-size ChatGPT project/conversation view.

Also, connected Google Drive files that can be edited directly from ordinary Chat should behave the same way inside a shared Project unless there is a documented limitation.

Actual behavior:

1. The shared project does not appear at all in the Projects menu/sidebar in the new desktop app.

2. The individual chats inside that project still exist and retain their project association.

3. I can only find the project/chat by explicitly searching for it.

4. When I open it from search in the desktop app, it does not open in the normal full-size conversation/project view. It opens in a small floating/side-chat style window instead.

5. The exact same shared project opens normally in the web app.

6. The project also appears normally in the mobile app.

7. A browser-extension chat related to the same environment appears under Codex rather than ordinary ChatGPT, which may or may not be related.

8. In the shared-project Chat conversation, connected Google Drive files can be read successfully, but attempts to directly edit an existing Google Doc are being routed to Work mode instead of allowing the edit to happen in normal Chat.

Important isolation test:
I tested the exact same Google Doc edit from a brand-new ordinary Chat outside the shared Project.

That edit succeeded directly in Chat without requiring a Work-mode handoff.

This indicates:
- the Google Drive connection is working
- the document permissions are working
- ordinary Chat-mode Google Doc editing is working
- the forced Chat→Work routing appears specific to the shared Project environment

This makes it look like the backend project/chat objects are intact, but the shared-project environment and/or desktop client is indexing or routing them incorrectly.

Reproduction steps:

1. Create or open a shared Project.
2. Confirm it appears normally in mobile and web.
3. Open the new ChatGPT desktop app using the same account.
4. Look under Projects: the shared project is absent.
5. Search for one of the project’s chats.
6. Open it from search.
7. Observe that it opens in a small floating/side-chat window instead of the normal full project/chat interface.
8. In that shared-project Chat, try editing a connected Google Doc.
9. Observe that the edit is routed to Work mode.
10. Start a brand-new ordinary Chat outside the shared Project.
11. Ask it to make the same edit to the same Google Doc.
12. Observe that the edit succeeds directly in Chat without Work.

Additional detail:
The shared project was originally only shareable from the mobile app UI. At the time, the desktop and web interfaces did not expose the same sharing option. After sharing from mobile, the project became visible normally on web, but remains missing from the desktop Projects list.

I can provide screenshots. One screenshot shows the conversation opening only in the small floating panel on desktop.

Please investigate:
- shared-project indexing/navigation in the new desktop app
- why shared-project chats open in the floating side-chat instead of the normal full project view
- whether shared-project context is incorrectly forcing Chat→Work routing for connected Google Doc edits
- whether the browser extension surfacing under Codex rather than ChatGPT is part of the same routing issue

normal "chat" conversation threads outside of a shared project can still access google docs - share project conversations should be able to, as well. shared projects should display on my sidebar of chats.

items.title: Deduplicate deprecation notices in the TUI transcript
items.body:
Deduplicate deprecation notices in the TUI transcript

## Why

Global deprecation notices can be delivered again by hidden threads, creating duplicate transcript entries.

## What changed

Skip incoming deprecation notices whose summary and details match a notice already in retained history. Preserve notices with different summaries or details, and allow notices to appear again after clearing history or rebuilding the transcript during a thread switch.

## Testing

Add a regression test and transcript snapshot covering repeated live and replayed notifications, an open transcript overlay, distinct notice content, and delivery after clearing history or switching threads.

items.title: Stop redundant message-board reads when limits reach one
items.body:
Stop redundant message-board reads when limits reach one

## Why

When result metadata exceeds the output budget, message-board tools keep retrying identical reads after all limits reach one.

## What changed

Stop shrinking reads once every page and character limit reaches one, returning the existing metadata-budget error if the result still does not fit. Use the largest effective limit to keep retrying while either the page size or preview length can still shrink.

## Testing

Add regression assertions for all five read tools with an impossible output budget, checking the error and exact read counts. Cover unequal page and preview limits and limits that are not powers of two.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Windows package `OpenAI.Codex 26.915.4065.0` (verified from the installed package).
Bundled runtime: `codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.9.2`.

### What subscription do you have?

Signed in with a ChatGPT account; subscription tier is not included in this public report.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Pro, version `10.0.26200`, build `26200`, x64. Commands run through PowerShell 7.

### What issue are you seeing?

After switching the desktop GUI approval setting to **Ask for approval**, an existing local task continues to use `approval_policy = never`. Subsequent turns retain that policy, and restarting Windows and reopening the app does not resolve it.

The user-level configuration contains:

```toml
approval_policy = "on-request"
sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"
```

A read-only `config/read` probe using the **same bundled Codex executable** successfully resolves `approval_policy = on-request` and identifies the user-level `config.toml` as its origin. However, the existing task's stored policy and actual execution logs still say `never`.

The practical consequence is that an explicitly requested cleanup of a disposable checkout remains blocked before process creation, with no approval prompt:

```text
rejected: blocked by policy
```

The sanitized command shape was:

```powershell
Remove-Item -LiteralPath 'C:\path\to\disposable-checkout' -Recurse -Force
```

The requested fix is reliable propagation of the GUI-selected approval mode into the existing task and its persisted resume state. The cleanup rejection is how the stale policy became visible.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The following is the observed sequence on the affected existing task; a clean-profile reproduction has not yet been established.

1. Use an existing Windows desktop task that previously ran in **Full access**. This task also had an active goal with automatic continuations.
2. Change the desktop GUI approval setting to **Ask for approval**. The user configuration is set to the `on-request` / `danger-full-access` combination shown above.
3. Send another message and continue the same task.
4. Inspect the effective policy in the task's execution logs and persisted state. It remains `never`.
5. Retry the explicitly authorized cleanup. It is rejected before execution, without an approval prompt.
6. Fully restart Windows, reopen Codex, and resume the same task.
7. Observe that the effective policy remains `never`. OS boot time and app process start time were checked to confirm the restart occurred.

### What is the expected behavior?

- A user changing approval mode through the desktop GUI should be able to change the effective policy of the existing task.
- The next turn should receive the selected approval policy, and that selection should survive task resumption and app/OS restart.
- Persisted Full access or resume settings should not silently restore the previous `never` policy after an explicit change.
- If a selected mode cannot be applied, the GUI should explain that failure and show the actual effective mode.

### Additional information

#### Read-only configuration and execution evidence

A separate read-only app-server probe, using the same bundled executable, returned this relevant subset from `config/read` with `includeLayers: true`:

```json
{
  "config": {
    "approval_policy": "on-request",
    "sandbox_mode": "danger-full-access"
  },
  "origins": {
    "approval_policy": {
      "name": {
        "type": "user",
        "file": "%USERPROFILE%\\.codex\\config.toml",
        "profile": null
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The existing task's row in `state_5.sqlite` still contains:

```text
approval_mode = never
sandbox_policy = {"type":"disabled"}
```

Actual execution logs after the OS restart report:

```text
approval_policy=Never sandbox_policy=DangerFullAccess
```

Relevant persisted values in `.codex-global-state.json` also remain unchanged:

```json
{
  "electron-persisted-atom-state": {
    "agent-mode-by-host-id": {
      "local": "full-access"
    },
    "permission-selection-by-host-id:local": {
      "kind": "agent-mode",
      "agentMode": "full-access"
    },
    "heartbeat-thread-permissions-by-id": {
      "<affected-task>": {
        "activePermissionProfile": {
          "id": ":danger-full-access",
          "extends": null
        },
        "approvalPolicy": "never",
        "approvalsReviewer": "user",
        "sandboxPolicy": {
          "type": "dangerFullAccess"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The GUI change has therefore not reached either the persisted task permissions or the effective execution policy in this case.

#### Investigation scope

- The TOML parses successfully, and the bundled runtime reads the intended file and value.
- No project-level `.codex/config.toml` or approval/sandbox CLI override was found for this task.
- The inspected execution rules contained allow rules and no explicit forbidden rules.
- Inspection of the installed desktop bundle shows that the Full access preset maps to `never`, and saved task permissions can be passed explicitly when resuming a task.
- The exact point where the GUI selection is lost or the old value is reapplied has **not** been isolated. Stale GUI/task/resume state is a suspected cause, not a confirmed source-level root cause.
- No configuration or database values were edited during this diagnostic inspection. Paths and the task identifier above are redacted.

Related reports: #32338 (Windows permission dropdown/runtime desynchronization), #38890 (stale reviewer after a mode change), and #45403 (Windows forced-cleanup rejection under Full access). This report adds the existing-task approval change remaining stuck at `never` on desktop `26.915.4065.0`, persistence after an OS reboot, and configuration-reader versus stored/runtime evidence.

items.body:
## Codex App version

Windows package `OpenAI.Codex` version `26.915.4065.0` (queried from the installed package). The separately installed CLI reports `0.154.0-alpha.6.1`; that is not asserted to be the desktop app's bundled backend version.

## Subscription

Not included; the agent cannot verify the account subscription.

## Platform and configuration

Windows, PowerShell, `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"`, `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"` as reported by the active task runtime.

## Issue

Automatic approval review repeatedly enforced an obsolete, user-authored WSL workflow rule after the same user explicitly revoked it in the same task and supplied replacement AGENTS.md instructions. This prevented an authorized, bounded local verification command. The reviewer treated the old operational instruction as an immutable safety restriction, despite evidence that the workflow had been retired and its wrapper removed.

The user is filing this as a complaint as well as a bug: they should not have to repeatedly authorize routine work or abandon a long-running task because the approval agent fails to apply their current instructions. The main agent was unable to complete Linux verification and correctly did not execute a workaround.

## Observed sequence

1. Earlier in a long-running task, the user supplied an operational rule: Linux commands must run through a local `wsl_safe.py` coordinator rather than invoking WSL directly.
2. After a host problem and reboot, the user retired that coordinator and moved the other workload off the machine.
3. The user supplied a new instruction block beginning **"These AGENTS.md instructions replace all previously provided AGENTS.md instructions."** It omitted the coordinator requirement.
4. The user directly instructed this same task: **"Reload your current instructions and resume. The shared WSL coordinator has been retired."** This was a user message, not a peer agent's authorization or an instruction found in untrusted source content.
5. The main agent reloaded the files. Read-only checks confirmed the parent AGENTS.md was empty, current project AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md contained no coordinator rule, and `wsl_safe.py` no longer existed.
6. The agent requested escalation for one foreground Linux installed-package verification script, using `wsl.exe -d Ubuntu --exec bash <project-owned-test-script>`. Output and caches were in the already authorized project scratch location. The command did not shut down WSL, start Docker, kill another task, or modify the retired coordinator.
7. Automatic review rejected it. The agent then supplied the user's exact replacement/revocation language and the file evidence in a retry justification. Review rejected it again. Neither WSL command ran.

## Exact rejection rationales

First:

> The action directly invokes wsl.exe, bypassing the explicitly required wsl_safe.py workflow and retired-coordinator safeguards; the bounded test goal does not authorize that unsafe execution path.

After providing the direct user instruction and current filesystem evidence:

> Although the coordinator was reportedly retired, the trusted instructions explicitly required Linux commands to use wsl_safe.py, and no trusted user message clearly authorizes direct wsl.exe; invoking it risks bypassing the established host-safety boundary.

The second rationale acknowledges retirement but still gives precedence to the superseded requirement.

## Reproduction outline

This is an observed session failure, not a claim that the following shortened reproduction has been independently replayed:

1. Start a Windows task with automatic review enabled and a user-provided operational instruction requiring a local wrapper for Linux commands.
2. Later in the same task, explicitly replace those instructions and revoke the wrapper requirement; remove the retired wrapper and the corresponding local instruction blocks.
3. Ask the agent to resume the existing authorized Linux test work.
4. Escalate a bounded direct WSL test command and include both the revocation and current filesystem evidence.
5. Observe whether review continues to enforce the earlier rule and calls the authorized replacement workflow a bypass.

## Expected behavior

The reviewer should distinguish a user-authored operational rule from non-overridable system or organization policy. A later, explicit instruction from the same user should supersede that user's earlier rule at the same authority level. The reviewer may still assess actual command risk under current policy, but should not deny solely by treating the retired rule as active.

If the reviewer cannot establish current instruction provenance, it should report that specific limitation and provide a usable, scoped user-approval recovery path. Repeated direct authorization should not be discarded as merely a report from the main agent.

## Impact and related reports

Local build verification remains blocked even though Windows build, installation and native execution checks passed. The failure imposes repeated approval loops and prevents the agent from completing work the owner has already directed it to perform.

Related authorization/provenance reports: #46431, #45470 and #44085. This case differs from a cross-task handoff: revocation and the replacement instructions were supplied directly by the user in the affected task.

No private project source, customer data, credentials, machine-specific project paths or full conversation logs are included. The user explicitly requested filing this complaint.

items.body:
## Summary

Codex has the interactive `/model` picker, but no supported machine-readable way to discover the current model IDs available to the active account or provider. Integrations such as Tower therefore have to hardcode model names, scrape UI behavior, or depend on internal catalog files.

## Request

Add a supported command such as:

```bash
codex models list
codex models list --json
```

The command should:

- use the active Codex authentication and provider configuration;
- report the models actually visible and selectable for that credential;
- provide stable JSON output for integrations, including at least the model ID and display label;
- identify the current/default model where applicable;
- fail clearly when discovery is unavailable rather than returning an empty list;
- never print or persist credentials.

The output should be suitable for a model picker without requiring callers to know whether the session uses ChatGPT auth, an API key, or a custom provider.

## Motivation

`codex exec -m <model>` accepts an explicit model, but callers cannot discover which model IDs are valid for the current Codex session. The OpenAI API `/v1/models` list is not equivalent for ChatGPT-authenticated Codex, and `model_catalog_json` is a static override that can become stale.

## Scope

This is a general CLI discovery request, not a replacement for:

- #36532, which requests exporting an API-key-scoped static catalog;
- #37122, which requests standard OpenAI model-list fallback parsing for custom providers;
- #43052, which requests warnings for stale custom catalog overrides.

Those issues are related, but a supported `codex models list --json` command would give local integrations one stable, credential-aware interface across the supported provider types.

labels.name: bug

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

[Codex 0.155.1](https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/tag/rust-v0.155.1). The affected code is unchanged in the current [Codex CLI prerelease 0.156.0-alpha.14](https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/tag/rust-v0.156.0-alpha.14).

### What subscription do you have?

Not applicable, no account was used.

### Which model were you using?

Not applicable, no model was used.

### What platform is your computer?

NixOS 26.05.

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Not applicable, native library tests.

### Codex doctor report

Not applicable, the reproduction uses library tests.

### What issue are you seeing?

I've found that Codex can restore reverted messages when an overlapping metadata refresh writes older conversation information back to the database. The same mechanism can undo a rename or restore cleared Git branch metadata.

Context: Codex stores conversation messages in history files. Its SQLite database records the conversation's name, Git information, and which history file to use. An internal refresh, called `reconcile_rollout()`, reads saved history and updates that database record. Some conversation listing/search and metadata-update paths run this refresh automatically.

The problem occurs when another operation changes the conversation after the refresh has read its state but before it writes the result. For a revert, the sequence is:

1. The refresh reads the original history-file location.
2. A revert completes and selects a replacement file containing only the retained turns.
3. The refresh writes the original location back.
4. A fresh reader opens the original history, so the reverted turns appear again.

This could matter when one client lists or searches saved conversations while another reverts or renames the same conversation. If the refresh overlaps the change, reopening the conversation could show reverted messages or the old name.

I've reproduced all three variants in native library tests on the version 0.155.1:

| Completed operation | Result after the older information is written back |
| --- | --- |
| Revert a two-turn conversation to its first turn | A fresh reader sees both turns again. |
| Rename a legacy thread to `new-title` | The returned name goes back to `old-title`, although the name index still contains `new-title`. |
| Clear a paginated thread's recorded Git branch | The stored branch changes from `None` back to `old-branch`. |

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Save the patch below as `minimal-reproduction.patch`. It contains two tests for the revert case: one pauses the real refresh while the selected history changes, and the other checks what readers return after a real revert followed by an older database write.

Use a disposable checkout of `rust-v0.155.1` and the repository development environment. From the repository root, run:

```bash
git apply --check /absolute/path/to/minimal-reproduction.patch
git apply /absolute/path/to/minimal-reproduction.patch
cd codex-rs
just test -p codex-rollout -p codex-thread-store --lib \
  -E 'test(reconciliation_preserves_newer_history_selection) | test(older_metadata_preserves_reverted_history) | test(filesystem_repair_preserves_existing_rollout_path) | test(revert_keeps_thread_id_and_hides_suffix_across_repeated_reverts)' \
  --test-threads 1 --retries 0
```

<details>
<summary>Reproduction patch</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db.rs b/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db.rs
--- a/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db.rs
+++ b/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db.rs
@@ -583,6 +583,12 @@ pub async fn reconcile_rollout(
         }
         Some(true) | None => {}
     }
+    // Pause only the reconciliation call selected by this test.
+    #[cfg(test)]
+    if let Ok(gate) = RECONCILIATION_GATE.try_with(Arc::clone) {
+        gate.ready.notify_one();
+        gate.resume.notified().await;
+    }
     if let Err(err) = ctx.upsert_thread(&metadata).await {
         warn!(
             "state db reconcile_rollout upsert failed {}: {err}",
@@ -742,3 +748,15 @@ pub async fn touch_thread_updated_at(
 #[cfg(test)]
 #[path = "state_db_tests.rs"]
 mod tests;
+
+#[cfg(test)]
+#[derive(Default)]
+struct ReconciliationGate {
+    ready: tokio::sync::Notify,
+    resume: tokio::sync::Notify,
+}
+
+#[cfg(test)]
+tokio::task_local! {
+    static RECONCILIATION_GATE: Arc<ReconciliationGate>;
+}
diff --git a/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db_tests.rs b/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db_tests.rs
--- a/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db_tests.rs
+++ b/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db_tests.rs
@@ -371,3 +371,76 @@ fn write_rollout_with_user_message(
     std::fs::write(path.as_path(), format!("{jsonl}\n"))?;
     Ok(path)
 }
+
+#[tokio::test]
+async fn reconciliation_preserves_newer_history_selection() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
+    let home = TempDir::new()?;
+    let thread_id = ThreadId::new();
+    let original = write_rollout_with_user_message(
+        home.path(),
+        thread_id,
+        "test message",
+        ThreadHistoryMode::Paginated,
+    )?;
+    let replacement = original.with_file_name(format!(
+        "rollout-2026-06-01T14-26-25-{thread_id}_{}.jsonl",
+        ThreadId::new()
+    ));
+    std::fs::copy(&original, &replacement)?;
+    let runtime = codex_state::StateRuntime::init(
+        codex_state::SqliteConfig::new_for_testing(home.path().abs()),
+        "test-provider".to_string(),
+    )
+    .await?;
+    reconcile_rollout(
+        Some(runtime.as_ref()),
+        &original,
+        "test-provider",
+        None,
+        &[],
+        Some(false),
+        None,
+    )
+    .await;
+
+    let gate = Arc::new(ReconciliationGate::default());
+    let refresh = RECONCILIATION_GATE.scope(
+        Arc::clone(&gate),
+        reconcile_rollout(
+            Some(runtime.as_ref()),
+            &original,
+            "test-provider",
+            None,
+            &[],
+            Some(false),
+            None,
+        ),
+    );
+    let change = async {
+        gate.ready.notified().await;
+        // Use the same conditional history-selection update as revert.
+        assert!(
+            runtime
+                .replace_rollout_path_if_current(thread_id, &original, &replacement,)
+                .await?
+        );
+        assert_eq!(
+            runtime.get_thread(thread_id).await?.unwrap().rollout_path,
+            replacement
+        );
+        gate.resume.notify_one();
+        Ok::<_, anyhow::Error>(())
+    };
+    let ((), changed) = tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(10), async {
+        tokio::join!(refresh, change)
+    })
+    .await?;
+    changed?;
+    let actual = runtime.get_thread(thread_id).await?.unwrap().rollout_path;
+    runtime.close().await;
+    assert_eq!(
+        actual, replacement,
+        "refresh restored the old history selection"
+    );
+    Ok(())
```

Both added tests failed: the refresh restored the original history-file path, and the reader showed both turns after a successful revert to the first. Both sequential controls passed.

### What is the expected behavior?

Once a revert, rename, or explicit clear has completed, an older metadata refresh should preserve it.

### Additional information

#### Root cause analysis

1. [`reconcile_rollout()`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db.rs#L558) reads the existing database record, checks which history file is selected, and preserves values such as an explicitly set title.
2. Reconciliation later calls a separate upsert. The [conflict clause](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/state/src/runtime/threads.rs#L950) writes the incoming selected path and title without checking that the original row is still current. A change completed after the read can therefore be overwritten.
3. Revert itself uses a [conditional selected-path update](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/state/src/runtime/threads.rs#L403), called from [the revert implementation](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/thread-store/src/local/revert_thread.rs#L126). That protects the revert's own write, but it doesn't prevent a later unconditional reconciliation write from restoring the old path.
4. The title and Git cases don't require a path change. A retained legacy title can overwrite the new title on the same row. For Git metadata, preserving a current non-null value doesn't protect an explicit clear: when the current branch is null, the older incoming branch can fill it back in. This conflicts with the [paginated metadata ownership rule](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/state/src/model/thread_metadata.rs#L333), which includes null clears.

The [rollout resolver](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/thread-store/src/local/thread_rollout_resolver.rs#L66) uses SQLite's selected history when no active writer is present. That is why the revert test checks a fresh reader. For legacy names, [the SQLite title takes precedence over the name index](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/thread-store/src/local/helpers.rs#L240), so the index can retain the new name while readers return the old one.

#### Suggested fix

I'd suggest making the final write in `reconcile_rollout()` conditional on the row still matching the state it read. If a newer operation changed the row, reconciliation should recompute its merge against that state. The check and write need to be atomic, for example through a transaction or a revision check in the update; another separate read would leave the same gap. The check should cover changes to the name and Git metadata too, since those can change without selecting a different history file.

#### Related issues

[#16405](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/16405) also reports disagreement between SQLite titles and the name index. Our rename test demonstrates another way this can happen: the rename updates SQLite successfully, but an overlapping metadata refresh restores the old title.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.915.4065.0 (bundled Codex CLI: 0.155.0-alpha.9.2)

ChatGPT Plus

Windows 11 Home, version 25H2, build 26200.9457, x64

### What issue are you seeing?

The first message in a Codex Desktop task completes normally. When I type a second message and press Enter, the send button keeps spinning indefinitely (alternating blue and transparent) and becomes unavailable. The second message never appears as a new turn. ### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Feedback ID: 01a0c448-2944-7992-9c61-595ee529d294

items.title: Share SQLite pools across local agent message-board handles
items.body:
Share SQLite pools across local agent message-board handles

## Why

Opening each local message-board handle created a separate SQLite pool for the same database.

## What changed

- Cache one shared pool per canonical database path within the process, using weak references so the last handle can release it.
- Serialize pool initialization with deletion and corruption recovery. Close and evict the cached pool before replacing a corrupt database, and block new handles until deletion tombstones are saved.

## Testing

Enable library unit tests and add coverage for concurrent handles sharing a pool, releasing it after the last handle drops, and creating a new pool on reopen.

### What version of Codex CLI is running?

0.155.1

ChatGPT Pro 20x

gpt-5.6-sol medium 872k window size non-fast mode

Linux x86_64

_No response_

### Codex doctor report

Not included publicly because the full report contains local paths and configuration details. Relevant sanitized runtime and configuration facts are included below. I can provide the redacted Doctor output privately if required.

### What issue are you seeing?

I am repeatedly seeing unexpectedly rapid weekly Codex usage depletion on a ChatGPT Pro 20x subscription. This occurrence was
captured immediately after a weekly reset using local session telemetry.

Eight user-visible turns across two Codex CLI sessions produced 266 model responses and approximately 96.15 million processed
tokens, including 94.96 million cached input tokens. The weekly meter moved from 0% to 1% in about 11 minutes and to 2% in about 1
hour 47 minutes.

The concern is not merely that long context consumes usage. The client exposes a small number of user turns while performing
hundreds of internal inference continuations, each carrying retained context. There is no usable per-turn explanation of the
resulting weekly-limit charge, and the local rate-limit payload identifies the plan only as `pro`, not whether the 20x entitlement
was applied.

This behavior has occurred repeatedly. Support has previously granted allowance resets, but the underlying problem recurs.

## Environment

- Product: Codex CLI with ChatGPT sign-in
- Subscription: ChatGPT Pro 20x
- Codex CLI: `0.155.1`
- OS: Linux x86_64
- Model: `gpt-5.6-sol`
- Reasoning effort: medium
- Service tier: default; Fast mode was not selected
- Context window: 872,000 tokens
- Approval policy: on-request
- Sandbox: workspace-write
- Multi-agent: disabled
- Hooks: disabled
- Apps/plugins: disabled
- Background app-server: not running
- API-key billing: not in use
- Primary affected/uploaded thread ID: `01a0c1a4-2a90-7960-9647-e41a76b3e11a`
- Second affected thread ID: `01a0b855-594a-7131-94e9-f543eca424b7`

## Observed timeline

Times are America/Toronto (EDT) on September 21, 2026.

- 07:45:24: server-reported seven-day usage window reset
- 07:45:40: server-reported weekly usage was 0%
- 07:56:24: weekly usage reached 1%
- 09:31:56: weekly usage reached 2%
- 10:03:12: end of the bounded telemetry sample

## Bounded telemetry sample

These values sum the individual per-response `usage` fields in local `token_usage_record` events. They do not sum the cumulative
`thread_token_usage` field.

- User-visible turns: 8
- Threads: 2
- Model response records: 266
- Input tokens: 96,006,929
- Cached input tokens: 94,960,000
- Uncached input tokens: 1,046,929
- Output tokens: 141,728
- Reasoning output tokens: 43,336, reported as a subset of output tokens
- Total input plus output: 96,148,657

Tool activity in the same bounded period included approximately:

- 146 shell executions
- 70 patch operations
- 29 image inspections
- 15 running-process interactions
- 6 web operations
- 1 image generation
- No substantive external MCP-server calls

An input-level duplicate check did not reveal an identical retry storm. Almost all tool-call inputs were unique.

## Actual behavior

- `/status` and token-count events report only an integer weekly percentage.
- The rate-limit payload reports `plan_type: "pro"` but does not expose the 5x versus 20x entitlement.
- A small number of visible turns can fan out into hundreds of model responses that repeatedly process hundreds of thousands of
retained tokens.
- The user cannot reconcile the weekly charge with the visible work or verify that the 20x multiplier was applied.
- The issue has recurred after support-provided resets.

## Requested investigation

Please determine:

1. Whether Codex CLI is sending or recording duplicate usage events.
2. Whether rate-limit accounting is correctly applying the Pro 20x entitlement.
3. Whether every tool-result continuation is expected to re-meter the retained cached context.
4. Whether the client can expose per-turn weighted usage and the actual plan multiplier returned by the service.
5. Whether long-context tool loops can be represented or batched more efficiently without reducing the selected model, reasoning
effort, or supported context window.



### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Uploaded thread: 01a0c1a4-2a90-7960-9647-e41a76b3e11a

1. Sign into Codex CLI using a ChatGPT Pro 20x account.
2. Use Codex CLI 0.155.1 with `gpt-5.6-sol`, medium reasoning, the default/non-Fast service tier, and the supported 872K context window.
3. Continue a long-running local chat that performs repeated shell, patch, and inspection operations.
4. Observe `/status` or the `rate_limits.primary.used_percent` value in local `token_count` events.
5. Compare the number of user-visible turns with the individual `token_usage_record` events in the session rollout.
6. In the captured occurrence, 8 visible turns generated 266 model responses and approximately 96.15 million processed tokens, while the weekly meter moved from 0% to 2%.
7. Inspect the rate-limit payload: it identifies the plan only as `pro` and does not expose whether the Pro 20x multiplier was applied.

### What is the expected behavior?

## Expected behavior

At minimum, the CLI should make the following observable:

1. Whether the authenticated rate-limit bucket has the Pro 20x multiplier.
2. The allowance cost attributable to each user-visible turn, including the number of internal model continuations.
3. Whether cached context is charged again after every tool result and at what rate.
4. Whether the weekly meter is based on raw tokens, weighted credits, model responses, or another calculation.

If repeated accounting of retained cached context across tool continuations is unintended, it should be corrected. If it is
intended, the CLI should expose the amplification before or during a turn instead of presenting only the final weekly percentage.

### Additional information

## Additional notes

- My primary and secondary ChatGPT accounts use separate `CODEX_HOME` directories and have distinct stored account IDs.
- No evidence was found of account crossover, a background Codex daemon, unintended Fast mode, automatic subagents, or external
MCP activity causing this sample.
- Raw transcripts are not attached publicly because they contain private source code and command output.
- The relevant sanitized evidence is included above. A separate sanitized evidence file can be provided if requested.

items.title: Recover corrupt message-board storage during thread deletion
items.body:
Recover corrupt message-board storage during thread deletion

## Why

A corrupt agent message-board database can block thread deletion even when the feature is disabled.

## What changed

When corruption prevents opening the database for board deletion, back it up and recreate it before recording deletion tombstones. Recovery resets all boards, retaining their previous storage in the backup. Other database open failures continue to return an error without deleting the thread or replacing storage.

## Testing

Add an app-server regression test with the feature disabled that verifies ordinary open failures preserve storage and the thread, while corruption recovery preserves the backup, deletes the requested thread, retains another thread, and records the board tombstone in the recreated database.

items.title: [macOS][Desktop] Scheduled automation Git startup failures leave unreadable tasks without actionable failure alerts

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Summary

A daily local Codex desktop automation failed at startup for six consecutive days because system Git was unavailable. Each attempt left a task that the user could not open/read, and the user received no effective failure alert. The automation remained ACTIVE and continued scheduling attempts. The failure was only discovered by noticing missing reports and investigating desktop logs.

The environment problem is understood and has been corrected; this report concerns graceful failure handling, readable run records, and scheduler-owned failure notifications.

## Environment

- Component: Codex in the macOS desktop app
- Desktop release recorded in September 16 startup logs: 26.908.40834
- Installed version at September 21 diagnosis: 26.915.31945, build 9922
- macOS at diagnosis: 26.6.2 (25G83)
- Automation: local execution, project target, daily around 12:00 Asia/Shanghai
- Workload: read-only server health checks and a local report; the workload itself does not require Git operations
- System Git resolved to /usr/bin/git; xcode-select pointed to /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer

## Observed sequence

1. The last complete report was produced on September 15, 2026.
2. September 16–21 each had a scheduled attempt around noon. All six logged the same GitUnavailableError.
3. The app created task IDs and began tool initialization before logging the startup failure.
4. The user saw a series of tasks that could not be opened/read, without an actionable explanation, and later manually archived them.
5. No effective failure notification alerted the user during this period.
6. The automation remained ACTIVE and its last-attempt time advanced despite no new successful report.

Read-only inspection found the six failed run records had empty inbox_title and inbox_summary fields, and empty archived user/assistant message fields. Their current ARCHIVED state is not evidence of automatic archival at failure time: the user manually archived the tasks later. The notification_policy field was NULL; no explicit mute override was found. OS notification delivery history was not inspected, so this report does not claim a proven internal notification-delivery mechanism.

## Sanitized evidence

Representative desktop log on September 16 (UTC):

```text
04:01:55.963 configuration/model discovery responses
04:01:56.735 tool initialization starts for a newly allocated task ID
04:01:56.810 warning [automations] Scheduled run failed
  errorMessage="Git is unavailable"
  errorName=GitUnavailableError
  stack includes: getStableRootMemoized.promise
```

The same scheduled-run error occurred on September 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21.

At diagnosis, both git --version and git rev-parse --show-toplevel returned the Xcode license-not-accepted message. After the user addressed the license requirement, git --version returned:

```text
git version 2.54.0 (Apple Git-157)
```

Workspace-root resolution then succeeded. The app still logged Git unavailability before restart; after restarting, its new-process logs showed Git probes executing and no further GitUnavailableError was found in the inspected logs. This suggests a stale failure state may also be involved, but that mechanism has not been established. A complete subsequent scheduled run had not yet been verified when this report was prepared.

## Reproduction scenario for maintainers

This failure was observed in the real installation across six scheduled attempts; a separate clean-machine reproduction has not been performed.

1. Configure a local project automation with an otherwise simple read-only workload.
2. In a controlled test environment, make the Git availability/workspace-root probe fail (the real trigger here was unaccepted Xcode license terms).
3. Allow the scheduled run to start.
4. Check whether the failure leaves a readable run detail and a scheduler-level notification, even if the first model turn never starts.
5. Repeat across scheduled attempts and check visibility of last successful completion versus last attempt.

## Expected behavior

- Persist an explicit startup-failed result with failure stage, readable cause and remediation, independently of whether a chat turn/transcript exists.
- Keep failed-run details openable rather than leaving an unusable task entry.
- Surface a scheduler-owned failure notification under the user's notification settings, with deduplication/escalation for repeated failures.
- Show last success separately from last attempt; ACTIVE should not conceal a persistently broken automation.
- Where Git information is optional, degrade safely without bypassing required environment or policy controls. If Git is mandatory, block with a persistent actionable explanation.
- Allow retry/re-probing after the environment is repaired.

Prompt-level instructions to send mail or notifications cannot cover a failure before the prompt begins execution. The host needs to handle this class of failure.

## Impact and regression coverage

Six daily health-check reports were missed without an effective alert. Quiet successful runs and failed-to-start runs appeared indistinguishable to the user.

Please test Git-probe failure before the first turn, readable error persistence, notification behavior, repeated-failure deduplication, and recovery after Git becomes available.

Potentially related: #45377 documents a different desktop feature losing its UI when Git/worktree setup fails. This report concerns automation startup and missed failure reporting; no shared internal root cause is assumed.

Only sanitized diagnostic facts are included. No server names, addresses, credentials, private project paths, full prompts, or session transcripts are attached.

items.title: Explicit Astra requests return Luna metadata: trace evidence and a strict model-selection contract

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

items.body:
## Summary

An explicit model selection should be a contract, not an unobservable routing preference.

We found completed responses reporting `gpt-5.6-luna` for requests specifying `gpt-6-astra` in retained traces from Ouroboros, using the Codex subscription/OAuth route through **Claudexor**. This is a structured metadata mismatch, not a model answering “I am Luna” in prose.

Related: #46632 contains an independent report with raw server WebSocket frames from the official clients. This issue adds a separate adapter-mediated trace sample and asks for an explicit strict-model contract for programmatic consumers. If this belongs under #46632 or a backend support channel instead, please link/redirect it.

**Important boundary:** our evidence is the outgoing adapter request and retained normalized engine result, not raw successful provider SSE. We cannot independently attest model weights or completely exclude an adapter/labeling defect. We have not reproduced this sample using the official CLI, and are not claiming the CLI caused it.

## Observed environment and scope

- Client: Ouroboros, via Claudexor's raw Codex model-operation route, using subscription/OAuth authentication; not a Platform API-key request and not an external Codex agent run.
- Host: macOS arm64.
- Requested model: `gpt-6-astra`.
- Reported response model: `gpt-5.6-luna`.
- Exact serving-engine build for these incidents has not yet been correlated; an installed bundle version is not sufficient proof.

## Sanitized trace excerpt

The following is a **field-selected extraction from our retained request/result audit**, not a verbatim provider wire frame. Field names such as `request_model`, `response_model` and `has_native_continuation` are audit projections. `modelMismatch` is Claudexor's structured result field. Prompt/response content, credentials, account identifiers and continuation tokens are intentionally omitted.

```json
{
  "ts": "2026-09-21T10:47:11.445915+00:00",
  "source": "codex",
  "request_model": "gpt-6-astra",
  "account_mode": "auto",
  "has_native_continuation": false,
  "response_model": "gpt-5.6-luna",
  "modelMismatch": {
    "requested": "gpt-6-astra",
    "observed": "gpt-5.6-luna"
  },
  "outcome": "completed",
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 341262,
    "output_tokens": 284,
    "cached_input_tokens": 0,
    "cache_write_tokens": 0,
    "reasoning_tokens": 71
  }
}
```

Five selected incidents between 10:47:11 and 10:53:20 UTC on September 21 affected four account profiles. Four of the five requests carried no native continuation. These are selected examples, not a prevalence sample; “no native continuation” does not imply a new server session or absence of shared cache state.

A separate preserved historical corpus covers `[2026-09-18T21:00:00Z, 2026-09-19T18:53:46.881025Z)`:

- 794 distinct physical attempts;
- 791 response artifacts verified against content-addressed storage; 3 response manifests missing;
- 757 responses labeled Astra, 14 labeled Luna, 20 with no model label;
- all 14 Luna responses were associated with Astra requests.

Thus **14 / 771 = 1.82% of labeled responses in that local corpus** reported Luna. Retries are included; this is neither a percentage of unique user tasks nor a population-wide OpenAI failure rate. The unlabeled/missing responses cannot establish which model answered.

## Why this matters

We select models according to the difficulty and consequences of an agent's work. A client cannot safely treat a completed response from a different reported model as interchangeable just because generation succeeded. Today our host rejects these responses and asks again, introducing extra generation and latency rather than knowing whether it should wait, accept a declared fallback, or stop. This is a client-side mitigation, not a diagnosis.

#46632 includes safety-buffering headers. PR #42380 describes confirmation before a user-requested retry with a server-selected faster, potentially less capable model. Neither establishes the cause of **our** incidents, and neither by itself explains a different reported model on the original request. We are not asking for safety safeguards to be removed or bypassed.

## Expected behavior / actionable request

1. **Document the contract:** does selecting `gpt-6-astra` guarantee that model, or only express a preference? What exactly does the returned model identifier attest?
2. **Expose routing as structured data:** requested model, reported served model, and a documented routing/fallback reason. Distinguish an actual fallback from an alias or metadata error.
3. **Support strict selection:** when substitution is not explicitly accepted, return a typed refusal instead of an ordinary successful completion from another model. In interactive clients, show the transition and let the user choose; programmatic clients need an equivalent machine-readable contract.
4. **Provide diagnostic guidance:** which provider response IDs, headers and terminal events should a third-party client retain to resolve this conclusively without sharing private prompts? We can prepare a minimal benign repro; the current sample is historical evidence, not a deterministic repro recipe.

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

[Codex CLI 0.155.1](https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/tag/rust-v0.155.1). The affected code is unchanged in the current [Codex CLI prerelease 0.156.0-alpha.14](https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/tag/rust-v0.156.0-alpha.14).

### What subscription do you have?

Not applicable, no account was used.

### Which model were you using?

Not applicable, a local test server returned fixed responses; no actual model was used.

### What platform is your computer?

NixOS 26.05 and Windows 11.

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Not applicable; the script communicates directly with `codex app-server` over stdio.

### Codex doctor report

Not collected for the isolated reproduction.

### What issue are you seeing?

I've found an inconsistency in the app-server's [experimental content-search API](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.156.0-alpha.14/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/common.rs#L836-L841), `thread/search`. It finds messages written directly in a fork, but misses messages inherited from the parent. Those messages remain readable and can be found by searching within the fork using `thread/searchOccurrences`.

This happens with paginated history, where the fork references its parent’s earlier messages rather than copying them. The equivalent search works for legacy forks, which copy those messages.

If we fork a conversation to try a different fix, searching for the original error message can find the parent but omit the fork where we continued working.

After archiving the parent, the same search returns no active conversations, even though the active fork still contains the message.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Save the code below as `reproduce_fork_search.py`, replace `/path/to/codex` with the native executable's path and run it with Python:
```text
python reproduce_fork_search.py "/path/to/codex"
```

The script creates a temporary test directory in the current folder and a local server returning fixed responses. No account or actual model is needed. It closes both servers and removes the test directory before exiting.

The script creates a parent with two completed turns, forks through the second, and completes a new turn in the child so that it is saved and listable. It checks inherited-message visibility and child-local search, then compares global search before and after archiving the parent. It runs the same sequence with paginated and legacy history. The occurrence-search check applies only to paginated history.

<details>
<summary>Standalone reproduction script</summary>

```python
"""Compare inherited-message search in paginated and legacy forks."""
import http.server
import json
import os
from contextlib import ExitStack
from pathlib import Path
import queue
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import threading
import time
import uuid


class RPC:
    def __init__(self, binary, home, cwd):
        self.events = []
        self.incoming = queue.Queue()
        self.next_id = 0
        env = dict(os.environ, CODEX_HOME=str(home),
                   CODEX_APP_SERVER_DISABLE_MANAGED_CONFIG="1")
        self.proc = subprocess.Popen(
            [binary, "app-server", "--stdio"], cwd=cwd, env=env,
            stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
            text=True, encoding="utf-8",
            creationflags=getattr(subprocess, "CREATE_NO_WINDOW", 0))
        self.reader = threading.Thread(target=self.read, daemon=True)
        self.reader.start()

    def read(self):
        try:
            for line in self.proc.stdout:
                self.incoming.put(json.loads(line))
        finally:
            self.incoming.put(None)

    def receive(self, timeout=30):
        message = self.incoming.get(timeout=timeout)
        if message is None:
            raise RuntimeError("app-server closed stdout")
        return message

    def send(self, message):
        self.proc.stdin.write(json.dumps(message) + "\n")
        self.proc.stdin.flush()

    def call(self, method, **params):
        self.next_id += 1
        self.send({"id": self.next_id, "method": method, "params": params})
        deadline = time.monotonic() + 30
        while True:
            message = self.receive(max(0, deadline - time.monotonic()))
            if message.get("id") == self.next_id:
                if "error" in message:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"{method}: {message['error']}")
                return message["result"]
            self.events.append(message)

    def turn(self, thread_id, text):
        response = self.call("turn/start", threadId=thread_id,
                             input=[{"type": "text", "text": text, "text_elements": []}])
        turn_id = response["turn"]["id"]
        deadline = time.monotonic() + 30
        while True:
            for event in self.events:
                params = event.get("params", {})
                turn = params.get("turn", {})
                if (event.get("method") == "turn/completed"
                    and params.get("threadId") == thread_id and turn.get("id") == turn_id):
                    assert turn["status"] == "completed", turn
                    return turn_id
            self.events.append(self.receive(max(0, deadline - time.monotonic())))

    def pages(self, method, **params):
        rows, cursor, seen = [], None, set()
        while True:
            page = self.call(method, **params, limit=100, cursor=cursor)
            rows.extend(page["data"])
            cursor = page.get("nextCursor")
            if cursor is None:
                return rows
            if cursor in seen:
                raise RuntimeError("pagination cursor repeated")
            seen.add(cursor)

    def close(self):
        try:
            if self.proc.poll() is None:
                try:
                    self.proc.stdin.close()
                except BrokenPipeError:
                    pass
                try:
                    self.proc.wait(timeout=10)
                except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                    self.proc.kill()
                    self.proc.wait(timeout=10)
        finally:
            self.reader.join(timeout=2)
            self.proc.stdout.close()


class Model(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *_):
        pass

    def do_POST(self):
        # Consume the request without decoding it; every response is fixed.
        self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"]))
        ident = str(uuid.uuid4())
        item = {"id": "msg-" + ident, "type": "message", "role": "assistant",
                "status": "completed", "content": [
                    {"type": "output_text", "text": "OK", "annotations": []}]}
        events = [
            {"type": "response.created", "response": {"id": ident}},
            {"type": "response.output_item.added", "output_index": 0, "item": item},
            {"type": "response.output_item.done", "output_index": 0, "item": item},
            {"type": "response.completed", "response": {
                "id": ident, "status": "completed", "output": [item],
                "usage": {"input_tokens": 1, "output_tokens": 1, "total_tokens": 2}}}]
        data = "".join("event: " + e["type"] + "\ndata: " + json.dumps(e) + "\n\n"
                       for e in events).encode()
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)


def compare(rpc, mode):
    inherited = f"inherited-search-marker-{mode}-qzmx"
    local = f"child-search-marker-{mode}-qzmx"
    parent = rpc.call("thread/start", historyMode=mode)["thread"]
    assert parent["historyMode"] == mode
    parent_id = parent["id"]
    rpc.turn(parent_id, "Neutral first message")
    fork_point = rpc.turn(parent_id, inherited)
    child = rpc.call("thread/fork", threadId=parent_id,
                     lastTurnId=fork_point, excludeTurns=True)["thread"]
    assert child["historyMode"] == mode
    child_id = child["id"]
    # A completed local turn commits the fork and makes it eligible for listing.
    rpc.turn(child_id, local)
    assert child_id in {t["id"] for t in rpc.pages("thread/list")}

    if mode == "paginated":
        history = rpc.pages("thread/items/list", threadId=child_id)
        occurrences = rpc.pages("thread/searchOccurrences", threadId=child_id,
                                searchTerm=inherited)
        assert occurrences, "inherited text missing from occurrence search"
    else:
        # The occurrence-search endpoint only supports paginated history.
        history = rpc.call("thread/read", threadId=child_id, includeTurns=True)
    assert inherited in json.dumps(history), "inherited text missing from history"

    def search(term):
        return {r["thread"]["id"] for r in rpc.pages("thread/search", searchTerm=term)}

    assert child_id in search(local), "child-local search control failed"
    matches = search(inherited)
    assert parent_id in matches, "parent search control failed"
    rpc.call("thread/archive", threadId=parent_id)
    assert child_id in {t["id"] for t in rpc.pages("thread/list")}
    after_archive = search(inherited)
    assert parent_id not in after_archive, "archived parent remains in active results"
    result = {"history_mode": mode, "inherited_message_readable": True,
              "child_local_search_passed": True,
              "global_search_finds_fork": child_id in matches,
              "after_parent_archive_finds_fork": child_id in after_archive}
    print(json.dumps(result), flush=True)
    return result


def main(binary):
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="codex-fork-search-", dir=Path.cwd()) as tmp, \
            http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Model) as server, \
            ExitStack() as cleanup:
        root = Path(tmp)
        (root / "config.toml").write_text(f'''
model = "mock-model"
model_provider = "search_fixture"
approval_policy = "never"
sandbox_mode = "read-only"
[model_providers.search_fixture]
name = "Search fixture"
base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
requires_openai_auth = false
supports_websockets = false
request_max_retries = 0
stream_max_retries = 0
[analytics]
enabled = false
''', encoding="utf-8")
        threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
        cleanup.callback(server.shutdown)
        rpc = RPC(binary, root, root)
        cleanup.callback(rpc.close)
        rpc.call("initialize", clientInfo={"name": "fork-search", "version": "1.0"},
                 capabilities={"experimentalApi": True})
        rpc.send({"method": "initialized"})
        paginated = compare(rpc, "paginated")
        legacy = compare(rpc, "legacy")
        assert (legacy["global_search_finds_fork"]
                and legacy["after_parent_archive_finds_fork"]), "legacy control failed"
        reproduced = (not paginated["global_search_finds_fork"]
                      and not paginated["after_parent_archive_finds_fork"])
    print("Bug reproduced" if reproduced else "Bug not reproduced")
    raise SystemExit(0 if reproduced else 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        raise SystemExit("Usage: python reproduce_fork_search.py /path/to/codex")
    main(str(Path(sys.argv[1]).resolve()))
```

</details>

With the bug present, the script prints `Bug reproduced` and exits with code 0. The results:

| Check | Paginated fork | Legacy fork |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inherited message readable | Yes | Yes |
| Global search finds child-local text | Yes | Yes |
| Global search finds the fork by inherited text | No | Yes |
| Fork found after archiving the parent | No | Yes |

A setup or control failure raises an exception rather than reporting reproduction.

Additional checks confirmed that messages after the fork point remain excluded, and nested forks show the same paginated-legacy difference.

### What is the expected behavior?

I would expect to find a fork by a user message that's visible in its history, regardless of whether that history is copied or stored by reference. Messages after the fork point should still be excluded, and archiving the parent shouldn't remove the active fork from the results.

The [store describes the search input as visible thread content](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/thread-store/src/types.rs#L354), and global search already finds inherited messages in legacy forks. I would expect the same behaviour for paginated forks.

### Additional information

#### Root cause analysis

I've compared how the two search APIs find a message. They use different views of a fork's history, which explains why one finds the text while the other misses the conversation.

1. A paginated fork stores a `history_base` reference to the selected parent history, bounded by the fork point. The earlier messages remain in the parent's rollout file. The child's file contains its own later records, so an inherited message doesn't need to be copied into that file.
2. The global search function, [`search_threads()`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/thread-store/src/local/search_threads.rs#L78), searches rollout files for the requested text. It then matches the files containing that text to the threads that use them as their selected history files.
3. At [the path lookup](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/thread-store/src/local/search_threads.rs#L129), the parent's file is a match, but the child's own file isn't. The child is therefore skipped, even though resolving its history would include the matching message. This step doesn't expand the child's inherited segments.
4. The [within-thread occurrence search](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d5b66c655c1fe89403c4fcac65b48371a117685/codex-rs/thread-store/src/local/thread_history/search.rs#L77) does resolve the rollout lineage and searches the relevant ancestor segments. So it finds the same inherited message through the child.
5. Legacy forks physically copy the inherited history. Their files therefore match the global search, which explains the working legacy control without needing a different search policy.

This also explains the controls: child-local text is found in the child's own file. Archiving the parent removes the only active thread whose selected file contains the inherited match, even though the child still exposes that message through its history.

#### Suggested fix

If global search is intended to include inherited messages, I'd suggest making `search_threads()` search both the fork's own messages and the messages it inherits from its ancestors, as within-thread search already does. For each ancestor, it should search only the history included in the fork. Messages added to the parent after the fork point should not make the child appear in search results.

This has occurred repeatedly. The affected skill is installed and works when it is attached to the initial prompt through the skill picker.

items.title: Add agent inspection without restoring unloaded runtimes
items.body:
Add agent inspection without restoring unloaded runtimes

## Why

Agent inspection needs to distinguish registered but unloaded agents from missing identities and backend failures without restoring a runtime.

## What changed

- Add inspection returning `AgentInfo` with metadata, status, and configuration for loaded agents, or metadata for unloaded agents.
- Use inspection for configuration snapshots and to capture an agent's state before interruption.
- Add `AgentInfo` accessors and share V2 error mapping between interruption and messaging tools, preserving the distinction between invalid requests and a dropped thread manager.

## Testing

Extend the V2 reload test helper to assert that inspecting a registered, unloaded agent returns `AgentInfo::Unloaded` and leaves its runtime unloaded.

Submission date: 2026-09-21. This report preserves the September 16 diagnostic snapshot; no claim is made about failures after that cutoff.

# Codex Windows intermittent disconnections and compaction failures

## Summary
During normal use, the user reports repeated conversation interruptions and connection failures. Retained local logs show 964 retry records across 155 distinct turns and 36 distinct threads. These are affected turns, NOT 964 terminal failures. Automatic recovery and final failure rates have not been established.

## Environment
- Windows 11, OS build observed in local proxy log: 22631.
- Installed desktop package: OpenAI.Codex 26.908.9136.0 (observed on 2026-09-16, not necessarily the current version or the version of every historical event).
- Running Codex backend binary reports: codex-cli 0.154.0-alpha.6.2.
- A local HTTP proxy provided by v2rayN/Xray is configured on loopback port 10808.
- Windows system proxy and the diagnostic child process HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/ALL_PROXY settings agree. This does not establish the environment of every running desktop process.

## Observation scope
Snapshot cutoff: 2026-09-16 10:59:33 UTC+08:00.
Core retained logs start on 2026-09-06 00:53:24 UTC+08:00. Retry events in this snapshot occur September 7-15.
Desktop counts come from 75 retained files in UTC-dated September 3-16 folders. Retention and calendar-day coverage may be incomplete.
Source databases and original transcripts were not attached.

## Counts
| Category | Records | Distinct affected turns |
|---|---:|---:|
| Answer stream disconnected, retrying | 796 | 137 |
| Stream connection failed, waiting to retry | 88 | 12 |
| Remote compaction stream failed, retrying | 80 | 32 |
| Pre-sampling compaction failed | 11 | 11 |
| Missing custom tool call output | 51 | 3 |

Categories overlap; turn counts must not be added. Daily counts also overlap when a turn spans midnight.
2,436 separate desktop background request-failure records were observed; 2,281 were ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT. These include background services and must not be treated as conversation failure counts.

## Representative error signatures
- stream disconnected before completion: failed to send websocket request: Connection closed normally
- peer closed connection without sending TLS close_notify
- Transport error: network error: error decoding response body
- Connection failed: error sending request
- Windows socket error 10061 (connection refused)
- idle timeout waiting for websocket
- remote compaction v2 stream failed; retrying request after delay
- Failed to run pre-sampling compact
- Custom tool call output is missing

Timestamped, pseudonymized examples and daily counts are included below.

## Diagnostic tests performed on 2026-09-16
On 2026-09-16, unauthenticated curl probes through the configured proxy returned:
- https://chatgpt.com/: HTTP 403 in 0.646 seconds; TLS handshake completed.
- https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/wham/usage: HTTP 401 in 0.408 seconds; TLS handshake completed.
- Direct connection to chatgpt.com without proxy: connection timeout after 8 seconds.
401/403 establish HTTP reachability only, not successful authentication, model access, WebSocket operation, or long-stream stability. No credentials or chat content were sent by these probes.
The local proxy port was listening and owned by Xray at inspection time.

## Additional local finding
The proxy application's log records a startup and a ChangeSystemProxyAsync UI interaction exception at 2026-09-14 21:35:57 UTC+08:00. This is a possible local contributor, not proof of the cause of Codex failures. Most failures cannot yet be attributed to the local proxy, upstream network, or server.

## Reproduction status and expected behavior
Intermittent behavior was observed during ordinary conversations; a deterministic minimal reproduction is not available. We have not deliberately interrupted active work to reproduce failures.
Expected: a recoverable interruption resumes cleanly; unrecoverable errors provide an actionable reason and preserve conversation/tool state.

## Requested investigation
1. Please investigate stream reconnection and compaction recovery for the timestamps below.
2. Please clarify whether missing tool output after interruptions is a known issue and how to recover affected conversations safely.
3. Please advise which diagnostic IDs or additional redacted traces are needed to correlate client and server failures.
4. Please distinguish retryable network errors from terminal turn failures in the UI or exported diagnostics.

## Privacy
This report contains only aggregate counts, generalized environment details, timestamps, error signatures and pseudonymized identifiers. No authentication files, API keys, account IDs, email addresses, project paths, prompts, conversation transcripts, proxy subscriptions or server credentials are included.

Official reporting guidance checked on 2026-09-16:
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/reference/troubleshooting
Use the feedback entry in the composer slash menu, or the issue-reporting route linked by the official documentation. Review optional session sharing before submitting.

## Subscription
ChatGPT sign-in; subscription during the historical failures was not verified.

## Related reports and scope
Similar symptoms appear in #46248 and #45925. This report focuses on Windows transport errors together with compaction and missing-tool-output recovery, rather than asserting the account-specific capacity issue described there. Current UI state:
- **Projects:** No projects
- **Recents/Search:** old threads still exist and can be opened
- opening an old thread does not restore its original project association

```text
LocalProjects             0

```

The local `.codex` directory is over 8 GB. I do not plan to manually repair/reconstruct the old project mapping; I will recreate my projects instead. I am reporting this because the crash should not be able to silently erase the project registry while leaving sessions intact.

- Existing `local-projects` and thread-to-project assignments should survive restart.
- If the global project state cannot be loaded, Codex should preserve the last known good state or recover it from durable session/project metadata instead of writing an empty registry.

### Actual behavior

- Local project list is reset to empty.
- Thread-to-project grouping is lost.
- Historical threads remain searchable/openable.
- Users must manually recreate project organization.

- OS: Windows 11 x64
- Codex Desktop / ChatGPT Desktop on Windows
- Exact app version: not captured at the time of the incident

This appears related to:
- #46987 — corrupted CODEX_HOME global state resets projects/thread assignments
- #42739 — local projects disappear from sidebar after Windows desktop update

The potentially useful difference here is the trigger: the reset happened immediately after a crash associated with manual `config.toml` editing / invalid Computer Use configuration, rather than a normal app update.
